section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Determinants as Area/Volume
section_1.content: Briefly define the determinant of a 2x2 matrix as the signed area of the parallelogram formed by its column vectors. This provides the spatial intuition needed to visualize how the system scales.
section_1.example: Visualize a unit square being transformed by a matrix; the determinant represents how much the area of the square has expanded or flipped.

section_2.title: The Linear System as Vector Scaling
section_2.content: Represent the system Ax = b as x(column_1) + y(column_2) = b. Explain that solving for x and y is equivalent to finding how much we must stretch/compress the basis vectors to reach the target point b.
section_2.example: A delivery robot starts at the origin; we need to find how many steps 'x' to take in Direction A and how many 'y' in Direction B to reach a package at coordinates (x, y).

section_3.title: Geometric Derivation of Cramer's Rule
section_3.content: Show that replacing a column in matrix A with the target vector b creates a new parallelogram. Demonstrate that the ratio of the area of this new parallelogram to the original determinant yields the specific coordinate value.
section_3.example: Visual animation: Show the original parallelogram (Area=Det(A)) morphing into a new shape (Area=Det(A_x)) as we swap the x-column with vector b.

section_4.title: Synthesizing the Formula
section_4.content: Formalize the visual intuition into the algebraic definition: x_i = det(A_i) / det(A). Emphasize that the determinant ratio acts as a 'scaling factor' that isolates one coordinate.
section_4.example: A side-by-side split screen showing the geometric area ratio on the left and the algebraic fraction on the right, highlighting their equivalence.

section_5.title: Constraints and Summary
section_5.content: Discuss the geometric implication when det(A) = 0 (the vectors are collinear, meaning the parallelogram has zero area). This confirms why Cramer's Rule fails for singular matrices.
section_5.example: A scenario where two robots move along the same line; the 'area' vanishes, and the system becomes unsolvable or has infinite solutions.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=20, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT, buff=0.3).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Map to right side of screen: Columns 1-6 map to x range [1, 6]
                x = 1.0 + j * 1.0
                y = 2.2 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
